profile: Opens a paragraph on the last one's point, often as a condition or consequence: 'If the signs are present and plain and yet we still pass them by, the fault is on our side.' / 'Placing the fault in the receiver has two consequences.' / 'Repair is only the start.'
Ends a paragraph on the point in a short, plain sentence, not an aphorism: 'In most of us, it is not working.' / 'Most of us see only the lamp.'

Explains a quotation or verse straight after it, often with a concrete inference: 'Cattle see and hear perfectly well, so the comparison cannot be about the senses. It is about what lies behind the senses.'

Leads into a verse with a one-line set-up that says what it will show: 'The Qur'an describes the gap in one verse.' / 'The Qur'an says where it lies, speaking of people who have every faculty and use none of them.'

Medium-short sentences; 'and' joins clauses without a comma; semicolons for balanced contrasts: 'God is not withholding signs; we are failing to receive them.' Occasional 'whereas': 'Eyes and ears take in the surface of things, whereas inside a human being...'

Brings in sources by full name with a specific verb, once per point: 'Sheikh Bahmanpour compares this faculty to a machine.' / 'Imam Khomeini insists...' / 'ʿAllama Tabatabaʾi explains...'; 'in the Sheikh's words' used sparingly, never 'he says' as filler

Speaks as 'we' / 'most of us' with the reader, inclusive and unscolding: 'We have heard these verses many times and we accept that there are signs in them'; 'Let's start with two claims'; almost no 'you'
Plain, concrete diction with everyday images: 'a person who sees a red light thinks of the danger it warns of, not of the colour and shape of the lamp'; 'There is a machine inside which is [rusted]'
Numbers and orders steps explicitly: 'The first is that the problem is not a shortage of evidence.' / 'The second is that the problem can be solved.'
Signposts to other chapters briefly and factually: 'Chapter Fourteen sets out their wider concerns, with the answers given to them.'
Never asks rhetorical questions, never jokes, never piles quotations without comment, never closes on a restated conclusion with 'then' or 'therefore' after the point is already made

tells: 'The scholars differ in emphasis but agree that powers are not the aim. Mutahhari also explains why seeking them would be shirk: the goal has become something other than God.' — restates the quotation just given; Author A would go straight on to what remains once powers are set aside

'...other than God Himself" and he recalls Imam ʿAli (as) saying that he worshipped God not from fear...' — a second source stacked on the first with 'and' and left unexplained; Author A brings in one source per point and comments on it
Chapter opening built like the reference's: prayer identified, 'when many of us hear it', what the line asks, then a plain link back to Chapter Two and a one-line statement of the chapter's task.
Opens on the previous point ('Pursuing ʿirfan means training the soul'), concrete examples of powers, and glosses 'shirk' straight after the quotation in a plain sentence.
Short concrete sentences, a cause given and then an example ('Allahu akbar or la ilaha illa Allah'); stops on the point about the guide.
One long paragraph stacking Mutahhari's quotation, a second quotation, the Khidr name and a verse of poetry — Author A gives one source per paragraph and explains it before moving on
'On either account, then, a traveller needs a companion who has walked the road.' — closing summary restating what was just said; Author A stops on the point
'The darkness ahead stands for the states of the soul that a traveller cannot read alone' — repeats the earlier wording ('cannot read alone') rather than moving the argument on
Picks up 'The second kind', concrete examples (hunger, pain, anxiety), semicolon contrasts; slight loss for the hunger-may-be-false aside, which does not prove completeness.
'Tabatabaʾi quotes a Persian couplet: "A thousand trap lies concealed..."' — claim, colon and quotation stacked, and the couplet is never explained; Author A comments after every quotation
'Tabatabaʾi gives a test' / 'Tabatabaʾi quotes' / 'he warns' — the source named in nearly every sentence; Author A names him once and then makes the point
'Both tests are needed because the road has many pretenders.' — the reason is asserted and then illustrated twice by quotation, more words than the point needs
Picks up the verse from the previous section, quotations glossed ('the Prophet ﷺ and the Imams (as)'), ends on a factual pointer to Chapter Fifteen; slightly heavy on quotation.

'There is nothing wrong with pursuing material wealth in this life; the trouble is being solely occupied with it.' — a true but moralising aside that does not move the argument; Author A does not lecture the reader on conduct
'The friends of God have families, friends and a place in society, as we do.' — adds a remark without advancing the point
'so that they understand far more' — vague closing gloss; Author A would say concretely what the removal of the veil gives

'the Sheikh sets it against' / 'The prophets, he says,' / 'the Sheikh says' / 'he grants' — the teacher named or 'he says' in almost every sentence as filler; Author A names him once and then speaks in its own voice

'The prophets knew God in this way, with a knowledge present in their hearts and not worked out by argument.' — closing line restates the paragraph's conclusion; Author A stops on the pointer to Chapter Four
Opens on the previous point ('Without a chain of authority'), plain contrast of order and Shia practice, Tabatabaʾi named once with a specific verb, ends on the verse it introduces.
Plain factual sentences, each prayer placed in time; sources brought in with specific verbs ('tells the traveller'); no flourish, though the opening 'God's invitation' is slightly grand.
Short contrastive sentence after the verse ('Most of us fear Allah's punishment...') mirrors 'Most of us see only the lamp'; verse set-ups name what each verse shows.

'The great teachers of the Shia tradition make closely related points, each in his own words.' — throat-clearing opener; Author A would open on the point itself ('ʿAllama Tabatabaʾi tells the traveller...')
Three quotations from Tabatabaʾi and one from Khomeini with no comment after any of them; Author A explains what each quotation shows
'Sheikh Bahmanpour calls Tabatabaʾi a symbol of Shia mysticism today.' — a true remark dropped in without moving the argument about the orders
'The teachers a Shia traveller can name therefore taught the road this book describes.' — tidy 'therefore' summary at the paragraph's end; Author A stops on the last concrete point (Qadi's half hour)
'Akhund Hamadani and those who learned from his line were scholars, several of them jurists and they stood outside the Sufi orders.' — loose 'and' chain joining separate claims
Quotation glossed word by word and tied back to Chapters One and Two; ends on the point. The Sheikh's aside about 'mistakes' is a slightly loose addition.
Opens with a condition picking up the last point; the quotation is followed by 'The sentence divides the work' and a semicolon contrast, as the reference explains its quotations.

'If the faculty can be repaired, there should be people in whom it already works' picks up the last point in Author A's conditional manner; the verse is explained by plain inference ('A heart trembles only at the mention of someone it has some experience of').
